result.question: Distinguish between the Himalayan and the Peninsular drainage systems of India with reference to their origin, nature of flow and the landforms they create. (Answer in 250 words)

sentences.text: India's rivers are commonly grouped into the Himalayan and the Peninsular drainage systems on the basis of their mode of origin, nature and characteristics.
The two differ sharply in age, regime and landforms.
The Peninsular drainage is much older, as shown by its broad, largely graded shallow valleys and mature rivers.
The Himalayan system, comprising the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins, has evolved along with the uplift of the young fold mountains.
Fed by both snowmelt and rainfall, Himalayan rivers are perennial, whereas most Peninsular rivers are rain-fed and seasonal.
Several Himalayan rivers, such as the Satluj and the Kosi, are antecedent and have carved deep gorges because erosion kept pace with the rise of the mountains.
On the plains they meander, form ox-bow lakes, flood plains and braided channels, and shift their courses frequently.
The Kosi, known as the 'sorrow of Bengal', is notorious for such shifts because of the huge sediment load it carries.
Peninsular rivers, by contrast, have fixed courses with few meanders, as they flow over the hard and stable Peninsular block.
Most of them, such as the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, flow eastwards owing to the block's tilt towards the south-east and build fertile deltas on the Bay of Bengal coast.
The west-flowing Narmada and Tapi, which occupy rift valleys, also build large deltas at their mouths.
The Western Ghats act as the main water divide, so rivers draining into the Arabian Sea are short and swift.
Perennial Himalayan rivers thus suit canal irrigation, while seasonal Peninsular rivers need storage reservoirs, a complementarity that inter-basin transfer plans must use carefully.
